question.text:
For the vector $\mathbf{u}=\begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 3 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}$ which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\mathbf{u} \perp H,\quad$ where $H=\left\{ \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \right\}$
  2. $\mathbf{u} \perp V,\quad$ where $V=\left\{ \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ \dfrac54\end{bmatrix} \right\}$
  3. $\mathbf{u} \perp W,\quad$ where $W=\left\{ \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 4 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \right\}$
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors of $H, V$ and $W$ as $\{\mathbf{h}_1,\mathbf{h}_2\}, \{\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2\}$ and $\{\mathbf{w}_1,\mathbf{w}_2,\mathbf{w}_3\}$, respectively.

Now, we have to compute the dot product between $\mathbf{u}$ and the vectors in each set.

  • For the set $H\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{h}_1 &= (-2) \cdot 2 + 3 \cdot 0 + (-4) \cdot (-1) = 0 &{\color{green}\checkmark} \\[3pt] \mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{h}_2 &= (-2) \cdot (-1) + 3 \cdot (-2) + (-4) \cdot 1 = -8\neq 0 &{\color{red}\times} \end{align*} So, $\mathbf{u} \not \perp H.$

  • For the set $V\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{v}_1 &= (-2) \cdot 3 + 3 \cdot 2 + (-4) \cdot 0 = 0 &{\color{green}\checkmark} \\[3pt] \mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{v}_2 &= (-2) \cdot 2 + 3 \cdot 3 + (-4) \cdot \dfrac54= 0 &{\color{green}\checkmark} \end{align*} So, $\mathbf{u}\perp V.$

  • For the set $W\mathbin{:}$ \begin{align*} \mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{w}_1 &= (-2) \cdot 0 + 3 \cdot 4 + (-4) \cdot 3 = 0 &{\color{green}\checkmark} \\[3pt] \mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{w}_2 &= (-2) \cdot 4 + 3 \cdot 0 + (-4) \cdot (-2) = 0 &{\color{green}\checkmark} \\[3pt] \mathbf{u}\cdot \mathbf{w}_3 &= (-2) \cdot 1 + 3 \cdot (-1) + (-4) \cdot (-2) = 3\neq 0 &{\color{red}\times} \end{align*} So, $\mathbf{u} \not \perp W.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating the Components of a Vector Orthogonal to a Set

question.text: Given that $\mathbf{u}=\begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \\ c \end{bmatrix}$ is a non-zero vector that is orthogonal to the set $W=\left\{ \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -4 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}\right\},$ find the value of $\dfrac{b}{a+c}.$
question.explanation:
The vector $\mathbf{u}$ is orthogonal to the set $W$ if $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}_1=0$ and $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}_2=0.$ So, we need to solve the following system:

\[ \begin{cases} \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}_1=0 \\ \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}_2=0 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} 2x_1-4x_2+2x_3 = 0 \\ 3x_1-2x_2+6x_3 = 0 \end{cases} \]

with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

\begin{align} M &= \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 2 & -4 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & -2 & 6& 0 \end{array}\right] & R_1 &:=\dfrac12 R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & -2 & 6 & 0 \end{array}\right]& R_2 &:=R_2+(-3) R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & -2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0& 4 & 3 & 0 \end{array}\right] \end{align}

In the reduced matrix above, we have $2$ pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd), so $x_3$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we get $x_2=-\dfrac34x_3.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain $x_1=-\dfrac{5}{2}x_3.$ So, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{5}{2}x_3 \\ -\dfrac34x_3 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_3\in\mathbb{R}. \]

Setting $x_3=4$, we get the vector $ \begin{bmatrix} -10 \\ -3\\ 4 \end{bmatrix}. $

Therefore, we obtain $a=-10,$ $b=-3,$ and $c=4.$

Finally, $\dfrac{b}{a+c}=\dfrac{-3}{-10+4}=\dfrac12.$

question.text: Given that $\mathbf{u}=\begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \\ c \end{bmatrix}$ is a non-zero vector that is orthogonal to the set $W=\left\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\-3 \end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}\right\},$ find the value of $\dfrac{b+c}{a}.$
question.explanation:
The vector $\mathbf{u}$ is orthogonal to the set $W$ if $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}_1=0$ and $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}_2=0.$ So, we need to solve the following system:

\[ \begin{cases} \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}_1=0 \\ \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}_2=0 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} x_1+x_2-3x_3 = 0 \\ 2x_1+x_2-x_3 = 0 \end{cases} \]

with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

\begin{align} M &= \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 1 & -3 & 0 \\ 2& 1 & -1 & 0 \end{array}\right] & R_2 &:= R_2 + (-2) R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 5 & 0 \end{array}\right] \end{align}

In the reduced matrix above, we have $2$ pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd), so $x_3$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we get $x_2=5x_3.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain $x_1=-2x_3.$ So, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} -2x_3 \\ 5x_3 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_3\in\mathbb{R}. \]

Setting $x_3=1$, we get the vector $ \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 5 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. $

Therefore, we obtain $a=-2,$ $b=5,$ and $c=1.$

Finally, $\dfrac{b+c}{a}=\dfrac{5+1}{-2}=-3.$

question.text: Given that $\mathbf{u}=\begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \\ c \end{bmatrix}$ is a non-zero vector that is orthogonal to the set $W=\left\{ \begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 0 \\ -10 \end{bmatrix}\right\},$ find the value of $\dfrac{a+c}{b}.$
question.explanation:
The vector $\mathbf{u}$ is orthogonal to the set $W$ if $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}_1=0$ and $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}_2=0.$ So, we need to solve the following system:

\[ \begin{cases} \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}_1=0 \\ \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}_2=0 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} 2x_1-x_2-2x_3 = 0 \\ 6x_1-10x_3 = 0 \end{cases} \]

with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

\begin{align} M &= \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 2 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 6 & 0 & -10 & 0 \end{array}\right] & R_1 &:=\dfrac12 R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & -\dfrac12 & -1 & 0 \\ 6 & 0 & -10 & 0 \end{array}\right] & R_2 &:=R_2+(-6)R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & -\dfrac12 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -4 & 0 \end{array}\right] \end{align}

In the reduced matrix above, we have $2$ pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd), so $x_3$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we get $x_2=\dfrac{4}{3}x_3.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain $x_1=\dfrac{5}{3}x_3.$ So, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{5}{3}x_3 \\ \dfrac{4}{3}x_3 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_3\in\mathbb{R}. \]

Setting $x_3=3,$ we get the vector $ \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 4 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}. $

Therefore, we obtain $a=5,$ $b=4,$ and $c=3.$

Finally, $\dfrac{a+c}{b}=\dfrac{5+3}{4}=2.$

The vector $\mathbf{u}$ is orthogonal to the set $W$ if $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}_1=0$ and $\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}_2=0.$ So, we need to solve the following system:

\[ \begin{cases} \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}_1=0 \\ \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}_2=0 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} x_1+5x_2-3x_3 = 0 \\ x_1+2x_2+2x_3 = 0 \end{cases} \]

with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

\begin{align} M &= \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 5 & -3 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 & 0 \end{array}\right] & R_2 &:= R_2 + (-1) R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 5 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 5 & 0 \end{array}\right] & R_2 &:= -\dfrac 13 R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 5 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -\dfrac 53 & 0 \end{array}\right] \end{align}

In the reduced matrix above, we have $2$ pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd), so $x_3$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we get $x_2=\dfrac 53 x_3,$ and from the first equation, we obtain $x_1=-\dfrac{16}{3}x_3.$ So, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{16}{3}x_3 \\ \dfrac 53 x_3 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_3\in\mathbb{R}. \]

Setting $x_3=3$, we get the vector $ \begin{bmatrix} -16 \\ 5 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}. $

Therefore, we obtain $a=-16,$ $b=5,$ and $c=3.$

Finally, $\dfrac{a-b}{c}=\dfrac{-16-5}{3}=-7.$

exampleAnswers.title: Identifying Which Vectors Belong to the Orthogonal Complement of a Set

question.text: Consider the vector subspace $H=\textrm{Span}\left\{\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ -2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 3 \\ -4 \end{bmatrix} \right\}.$ Which of the following vectors belong to $H^{\perp}?$ \[ \mathbf{v}_1=\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{v}_2=\begin{bmatrix} -4 \\ 5 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix},\qquad \mathbf{v}_3=\begin{bmatrix} -7 \\ 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors that span the subspace $H$ as $\mathbf{h}_1$ and $\mathbf{h}_2.$

Now, a vector $\mathbf{v}$ belongs to $H^{\perp}$ if $\mathbf{v}$ is orthogonal to the set of vectors that spans the subspace $H.$ So, we have to find the products $\mathbf{v}_i \cdot \mathbf{h}_j$ for $i=1,2,3 $ and $j=1,2.$

  • For $\mathbf{v}_1$, we have the following: \begin{align*} \mathbf{v}_1 \cdot \mathbf{h}_1 &= 2\cdot (-1)+2\cdot(-2)+3\cdot 2 = 0 &\quad{\color{green}\checkmark} \\[3pt] \mathbf{v}_1 \cdot \mathbf{h}_2 &= 2\cdot 3+2\cdot 3+3\cdot(-4) = 0 & \quad{\color{green}\checkmark} \end{align*} So, $\mathbf{v}_1\in H^{\perp}.$

  • For $\mathbf{v}_2$, we have the following:
    \begin{align*} \mathbf{v}_2 \cdot \mathbf{h}_1 &= (-4)\cdot (-1)+5\cdot(-2)+3\cdot 2 = 0 &\quad{\color{green}\checkmark} \\[3pt] \mathbf{v}_2 \cdot \mathbf{h}_2 &= (-4)\cdot 3+5\cdot 3+3\cdot (-4) = -9 \neq 0 & \quad{\color{red}\times} \end{align*} So, $\mathbf{v}_2\notin H^{\perp}.$

  • For $\mathbf{v}_3$, we have the following:
    \begin{align*} \mathbf{v}_3 \cdot \mathbf{h}_1 &= (-7)\cdot (-1)+2\cdot(-2)+1\cdot 2 = 5 \neq 0 & \quad{\color{red}\times} \end{align*} So, $\mathbf{v}_3 \notin H^{\perp}.$ We do not need to test $\mathbf v_3\cdot \mathbf h_2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$\mathbf{v}_1$ only."

  • For $\mathbf{v}_1$, we have the following: \begin{align*} \mathbf{v}_1 \cdot \mathbf{h}_1 &= 9 \cdot 2 + (-2) \cdot 5 + 4 \cdot 7 = 36 \neq 0 &{\color{red}\times} \end{align*} So, $\mathbf{v}_1 \notin H^{\perp}.$ We do not need to test $\mathbf v_1\cdot \mathbf h_2.$

  • For $\mathbf{v}_2$, we have the following: \begin{align*} \mathbf{v}_2 \cdot \mathbf{h}_1 &= 9 \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot 5 + (-4) \cdot 7 = 0 &{\color{green}\checkmark} \\[5pt] \mathbf{v}_2 \cdot \mathbf{h}_2 &= 9 \cdot 0 + 2 \cdot 2 + (-4) \cdot 1 = 0 &{\color{green}\checkmark} \end{align*} So, $\mathbf{v}_2 \in H^{\perp}.$

  • For $\mathbf{v}_3$, we have the following: \begin{align*} \mathbf{v}_3 \cdot \mathbf{h}_1 &= 3 \cdot 2 + (-2) \cdot 5 + 4 \cdot 7 = 24 \neq 0 &{\color{red}\times} \end{align*} So, $\mathbf{v}_3 \notin H^{\perp}.$ We do not need to test $\mathbf v_3\cdot \mathbf h_2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$\mathbf{v}_2$ only".

  • For $\mathbf{v}_3$, we have the following: \begin{align*} \mathbf{v}_3 \cdot \mathbf{h}_1 &= (-1) \cdot 2 + 2 \cdot (-1) + (-2) \cdot (-1) = -2 \neq 0 &{\color{red}\times} \end{align*} So, $\mathbf{v}_3 \notin H^{\perp}.$ We do not need to test $\mathbf v_3\cdot \mathbf h_2.$

exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Orthogonal Complement of a Span

question.text: Find $H^{\perp}$, if $H=\textrm{Span}\left\{\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix} 9 \\ -6 \end{bmatrix} \right\}.$
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors that span the subspace $H$ as $\mathbf{h}_1$ and $\mathbf{h}_2.$

A vector $\mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}$ belongs to $H^{\perp}$ if $\mathbf{x}\cdot \mathbf{h}_1=0$ and $\mathbf{x}\cdot \mathbf{h}_2=0.$ So, we need to solve the following system: \[ \begin{cases} \mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{h}_1=0 \\ \mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{h}_2=0 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} 3x_1-2x_2 = 0 \\ 9x_1-6x_2 = 0 \end{cases} \]

with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form as follows:

\begin{align} M &= \left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 3 & -2 & 0 \\ 9 & -6 & 0 \end{array}\right] & R_2 &:= R_2 - 3R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 3 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{array}\right] \end{align}

In the reduced matrix above, we have $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one), so $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we get $x_1=\dfrac{2}{3}x_2.$ So, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{3}x_2 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2\in\mathbb{R}. \]

Therefore, our orthogonal complement is \[ H^{\perp} = \left\{ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{3}x_2 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix} \: : \: x_2\in\mathbb{R}\right\}. \]

example.title: Finding the Orthogonal Complement of a Span

question.text: Find a basis of $H^{\perp}$ if $H=\textrm{Span}\left\{\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -2 \\5\end{bmatrix} \right\}.$
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vector that spans the subspace $H$ as $\mathbf{h}_1.$

A vector $\mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}$ belongs to $H^{\perp}$ if $\mathbf{x}\cdot \mathbf{h}_1=0.$ So, we need to solve the following system:

\[ \begin{cases} \mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{h}_1=0 \\ \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} 4x_1-2x_2+5x_3 = 0 \end{cases} \]

with the augmented matrix $M,$ which is already in row echelon form:

\begin{align} M &= \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 4 & -2 & 5 & 0 \\ \end{array}\right] \end{align}

In the reduced matrix above, we have $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one), so $x_2$ and $x_3$ are free variables. From the equation, we get $x_1=\dfrac{1}{4}(2x_2-5x_3).$ So, every vector in $H^{\perp}$ has the form \[ \begin{bmatrix}\dfrac{1}{4}(2x_2-5x_3) \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix} = x_2 \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{2} \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}+x_3\begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac 54 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2, x_3\in\mathbb{R}. \]

Therefore, $\mathcal{B}=\left\{\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{2} \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac 54 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\right\}$ is a basis of $H^{\perp}.$

question.text: Find a basis of $H^{\perp}$ if $H=\textrm{Span}\left\{\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ -2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} \right\}.$
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vector that spans the subspace $H$ as $\mathbf{h}_1.$

A vector $\mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}$ belongs to $H^{\perp}$ if $\mathbf{x}\cdot \mathbf{h}_1=0.$ So, we need to solve the following system:

\[ \begin{cases} \mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{h}_1=0 \\ \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} 5x_1-2x_2+3x_3 = 0 \end{cases} \]

with the augmented matrix $M,$ which is already in row echelon form:

\begin{align} M &= \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 5 & -2 & 3 & 0 \\ \end{array}\right] \end{align}

In the reduced matrix above, we have $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one), so $x_2$ and $x_3$ are free variables. From the equation, we get $x_1=\dfrac{2}{5}x_2-\dfrac{3}{5}x_3.$ So, every vector in $H^{\perp}$ has the form \[ \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{5}x_2-\dfrac{3}{5}x_3 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix} = x_2 \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{5} \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}+x_3\begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{3}{5} \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2, x_3\in\mathbb{R}. \]

Therefore, $\mathcal{B}=\left\{\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{5} \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{3}{5} \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\right\}$ is a basis of $H^{\perp}.$

example.title: Finding the Orthogonal Complement of a Span

question.text: Find a basis of $H^{\perp}$ if $H=\textrm{Span}\left\{\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\2\end{bmatrix} \right\}.$
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vector that spans the subspace $H$ as $\mathbf{h}_1.$

A vector $\mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix}$ belongs to $H^{\perp}$ if $\mathbf{x}\cdot \mathbf{h}_1=0.$ So, we need to solve the following system:

\[ \begin{cases} \mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{h}_1=0 \\ \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} 2x_1-x_2+2x_3 = 0 \end{cases} \]

with the augmented matrix $M,$ which is already in row echelon form:

\begin{align} M &= \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 2 & -1 & 2 & 0 \\ \end{array}\right] \end{align}

In the reduced matrix above, we have $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one), so $x_2$ and $x_3$ are free variables. From the equation, we get $x_1=\dfrac{1}{2}(x_2-2x_3).$ So, every vector in $H^{\perp}$ has the form \[ \begin{bmatrix}\dfrac{1}{2}(x_2-2x_3) \\ x_2 \\ x_3 \end{bmatrix} = x_2 \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{2} \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}+x_3\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2, x_3\in\mathbb{R}. \]

Therefore, $\mathcal{B}=\left\{\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{2} \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\right\}$ is a basis of $H^{\perp}.$

example.title: Finding the Orthogonal Complement of a Span

question.text: Find $H^{\perp}$, if $H=\textrm{Span}\left\{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} \right\}.$
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors that span the subspace $H$ as $\mathbf{h}_1$ and $\mathbf{h}_2.$

A vector $\mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}$ belongs to $H^{\perp}$ if $\mathbf{x}\cdot \mathbf{h}_1=0$ and $\mathbf{x}\cdot \mathbf{h}_2=0.$ So, we need to solve the following system: \[ \begin{cases} \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{h}_1=0 \\ \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{h}_2=0 \end{cases} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \begin{cases} x_1+2x_2 = 0 \\ 2x_1-x_2 = 0 \end{cases} \]

with the augmented matrix $M,$ which we reduce to row echelon form as follows:

\begin{align} M &= \left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 \end{array}\right] & R_2 &:= R_2 -{2}R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0 \end{array}\right] \end{align}

In the reduced matrix above, we have $2$ pivot columns. From the second equation, we get $ x_2 = 0$ and from the first one, we obtain $ x_1 = 0. $ So, the solution to the system is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}=\mathbf{0} \]

Therefore, our orthogonal complement is \[ H^{\perp} = \left\{\mathbf{0}\right\}. \]
